w: 1 Vertical incisions at the line angle, never through the papilla A professor's hint · 3 questions in the bank Know this Confirmed as a literal quiz question: a flap's base must be wider than its coronal edge, or the flap starves the tissue it's still attached to of blood supply. When intrasulcular or crestal alone doesn't give enough exposure — most major augmentations — a vertical (releasing) incision is dropped at the line angle of a tooth to open a bigger flap without having to include more teeth in the horizontal incision. One vertical incision plus intrasulcular across three teeth (say, distal of #7 with intrasulcular on 7-8-9) makes a triangular pyramidal flap — enough exposure for implant placement with an onlay graft. Two verticals, one on each side of the defect, make a trapezoidal flap, needed for major vertical augmentation because two releases let the flap coronally advance with passive, tension-free closure over a graft — something a single vertical often can't stretch to do without tearing. Every incision and flap in this course answers to the same five rules: a firm, continuous stroke rather than several tentative passes; keeping the incision at a distance from the actual lesion or bony defect rather than cutting directly over it; placing vertical incisions at the line angle of the tooth; reflecting the periosteum as an integral part of the flap; and keeping the base of the flap at least as wide as its free edge, since a narrow base starves the flap of the only blood supply it has left once it's reflected. 2 A flap's base must be wider than its free edge A professor's hint · 3 questions in the bank Beyond how it's opened, a flap is classified along three more axes: how much bone is exposed on reflection (full-thickness, taking the periosteum with it, versus split-thickness, leaving periosteum on the bone), where it's repositioned after surgery (coronal to the CEJ for soft-tissue augmentation, or apical for crown lengthening and osseous surgery), and whether the papilla is preserved intact or not. A sulcular flap — intrasulcular incision only, no vertical release — gives the most limited access of the group and is hard to advance because the tissue stays attached laterally; it's the first, smallest option, reached for on minor augmentation or a single implant. Extending it to include one more tooth on each side (still no vertical) buys moderate additional access without escalating to a releasing incision at all. 3 The sub-marginal incision A professor's hint · 2 questions in the bank Know this Sub-marginal incision was added to the in-class follow-up at another instructor's explicit request — treat it as testable even though the original recording only promised depth on intrasulcular/crestal and vertical incisions. Confirmed as a literal quiz question: vertical incisions go at the line angle, never through the papilla — placing one mid-papilla risks a black triangle, placing one off the line angle risks recession. The in-class review added a fourth named incision that doesn't fit the reflect-and-close pattern of the other three: the sub-marginal incision, placed below the free gingival margin (the "sub" is literal — below the margin) rather than in the sulcus or on the crest. Where intrasulcular/crestal and vertical incisions are about gaining access and are designed to be closed back to their original position, a sub-marginal incision is deliberately excisional: it's scalloped through the pocket wall itself and the tissue coronal to it is removed outright, not reflected and repositioned. The point is pocket elimination in resective/osseous surgery — if a site probes 6 mm against a 3 mm normal, cutting roughly 3 mm of pocket wall away leaves the patient with a shallower, cleansable sulcus instead of a deep one that will keep repopulating with pathogens between maintenance visits. The tradeoff is intentional: this incision creates recession by design (the gingival margin ends up higher after healing), which is the right call when the alternative is an unmaintainable periodontal pocket, but the wrong call — and never attempted — on a site being treated for recession instead of pocket depth. Whether recession should be created or corrected at a given site always comes back to what the actual problem is: a deep pocket calls for a sub-marginal incision, thin/receded tissue calls for grafting, and the two aren't contradictory approaches, just answers to different problems. 4 The suture chart: resorption, braided vs monofilament, tissue reaction Midterm check-ins · 8 questions in the bank The course's own material comparison chart sorts six specific materials along the same two axes — natural vs. synthetic, monofilament vs. braided — plus resorption time, strength, tissue reaction, and handling (full chart in Reference Tables). Chromic gut is natural, monofilament, and resorbs fastest (7–10 days) but handles very poorly; it's reached for at extraction sites, implants without additional grafting, or to stabilize a collagen membrane. The two synthetic resorbables split by construction: PGA is braided, resorbs slowest of the resorbables (55–70 days), handles beautifully, but irritates tissue — a fit for ridge and sinus augmentation where healing takes a while. PGCL is monofilament, resorbs faster (22–55 days), and is gentler on tissue, making it the choice for soft-tissue grafting and esthetic crown lengthening. Among the non-resorbables, poly-propylene behaves like nylon with no tissue adherence; silk handles beautifully but causes the worst tissue reaction of any material on the list and must be physically removed at 7 days; PTFE is the highest-cost option and is used across nearly every surgery type except pure soft-tissue grafts. 5 Suture techniques from a picture Midterm check-ins · 9 questions in the bank Single interrupted sutures (with the figure-8 variant) are the general-purpose default, each throw tied independently. Horizontal mattress sutures are essential for larger bone-augmentation procedures and prevent flap-margin inversion, but overtightening constricts blood supply to the incision edge and risks bone necrosis and dehiscence. Vertical mattress sutures maximize tissue approximation and eversion, and are the go-to for approximating papillae in the esthetic zone or closing an oro-antral communication. Continuous and continuous-locking sutures place bites close together for a strong seal, but the entire line can come undone if a single throw fails — a real risk with monofilament or other high-glide materials — and are typically reserved for edentulous long-span areas, alveoloplasties, and apicoectomies. Sling and periosteal-anchorage sutures round out the technique list for repositioning a flap around a single tooth or anchoring it apically or laterally. 6 Full vs partial thickness by procedure Core of the lecture · 4 questions in the bank The full-vs-split decision has a simple test behind it: if the surgical goal involves bone in any way, reflect full thickness and expose it; if the goal is purely soft tissue, go split thickness and leave the periosteum behind as a vascularized bed. That single rule covers every case the course walks through — implant placement, bone/ridge/sinus augmentation, and crown lengthening or osseous surgery (all bone-related) are full-thickness; soft-tissue grafting is the one split-thickness exception, precisely because a split-thickness bed is what lets the graft's blood vessels anastomose with the recipient site's own vessels during healing. Also flagged in class Expect case-based reasoning rather than a single memorized "correct" answer for incision/flap/suture choice — be ready to justify a defensible option, the same case-based exam style as Session 1. You can skip Study intrasulcular/crestal and vertical incisions in depth — other incision families were named only in passing and aren't where this lecture's testing weight sits.
